title: A 380-Million-Year-Old Fish Skull Reveals Brain Adaptations for the Water-to-Land Transition
summary: Around 385 million years ago, in the shallow freshwater systems of the supercontinent Gondwana, a meter-long ambush predator lurked. Koharalepis jarviki was a lobe-finned fish, a close relative of the first vertebrates that would eventually drag themselves onto land. Now, a new study from Flinders University has unlocked secrets hidden inside its fossilized skull, thanks to advanced neutron imaging that allowed scientists to see internal structures without damaging the precious specimen. The fossil, discovered in Antarctica's Lashly Mountains, is the only known example of its species and the sole member of the Canowindridae family to preserve the internal bones of the skull. "We chose to focus on Koharalepis as it is the only fossil in the entire family to preserve the internal bones of the skull, which gives us valuable insights into its braincase and neuroanatomy," says lead author Corinne Mensforth, a PhD candidate at the Flinders Palaeontology Lab. What they found was striking: the fish's brain shared key similarities with those of tetrapod-like fishes that straddle the evolutionary transition from water to land. The scans revealed adaptations for life near the water's surface, including openings in the top of the skull for additional air intake—essentially a built-in snorkel. Inside the braincase, researchers identified a pineal organ, a light-sensitive structure that helps regulate circadian rhythms, suggesting Koharalepis was attuned to day-night cycles. With relatively small eyes, the fish likely relied on other senses to hunt, making it a formidable ambush predator. "This precious fossil belongs to a group called the Canowindridae which highlights the ancient links between Australia and Antarctica," explains Dr. Alice Clement, a research fellow at Flinders and coauthor of the study published in Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution. During the Devonian, these landmasses were connected as part of East Gondwana, and fossils from this family have been found in both regions. The findings add a crucial piece to the puzzle of how vertebrates evolved from aquatic creatures into land-dwelling tetrapods. By understanding the sensory and respiratory adaptations in Koharalepis, scientists can better trace the incremental changes that allowed our distant ancestors to take their first steps on solid ground.
why_it_matters: The shift from water to land is one of the most pivotal events in our own evolutionary history; the adaptations seen in Koharalepis – such as air intake openings and brain structures – are clues to how our distant fish ancestors could eventually breathe air and navigate a completely different environment, setting the stage for all land vertebrates including humans.

background_read: The Devonian Period, often called the 'Age of Fishes,' lasted from about 419 to 359 million years ago; during this time, the first tetrapods (four-limbed vertebrates) began to evolve from lobe-finned fish.
Gondwana was a massive southern supercontinent; the fossil's location in Antarctica and the presence of related Canowindridae fish in Australia show these landmasses were once connected.

Flinders University in South Australia is a leader in palaeontology, and its researchers used neutron imaging—a technique usually applied to engineering materials—to non-destructively scan the rare skull.
Lobe-finned fish like Koharalepis possess fleshy fins with bones similar to the upper arm, forearm, and wrist of land animals, making them key to understanding the water-to-land transition.

The pineal organ, found in the brain of many lower vertebrates, is sensitive to light and regulates daily rhythms; its presence suggests this fish was tuned to day-night cycles, perhaps to coordinate hunting or surface breathing.
Article_Structure: LEAD: A fossil fish skull from 385 million years ago, found in Antarctica, reveals internal brain structures that shed light on the water-to-land transition.
└─ WHO: Lead author Corinne Mensforth and coauthor Dr. Alice Clement from Flinders University.
KEY FINDING: Using neutron imaging, researchers uncovered adaptations for life near the water's surface and brain features shared with tetrapod-like fishes.
├─ ANATOMY: Openings on top of the skull served as a 'built-in snorkel' for extra air intake.
├─ NEUROANATOMY: A well-defined pineal organ suggests sensitivity to light and regulation of circadian rhythms.
└─ SENSORY TRADE-OFF: Small eyes imply the fish relied on other senses, consistent with ambush predation.
EVOLUTIONARY LINK: Koharalepis belongs to the Canowindridae family, whose fossils in Antarctica and Australia underscore ancient Gondwanan connections.
└─ IMPORTANCE: As the only Canowindridae fossil preserving internal skull bones, it provides direct evidence of neuroanatomical changes preceding the move to land.
IMPLICATIONS: The study fills a gap in understanding how incremental sensory and respiratory adaptations paved the way for vertebrate life on land.

perspectives.description: This rare fossil gives palaeontologists a direct look at the internal skull of a near-tetrapod fish, helping to test hypotheses about how the brain and sensory systems changed during the transition to land. Neutron imaging preserves the only specimen of its kind for future study.

Relying on a single fossil means we can't be certain these features represent the whole species; individual variation or preservation biases could distort the picture. There is also a risk of over-interpreting soft-tissue structures from bone impressions alone.

Evolution rarely happens in huge leaps; the mosaic of aquatic and surface features in Koharalepis fits a broader pattern where transitional forms accumulate small adaptations over millions of years. Its combination of an air-snorkel, small eyes, and a light-sensitive pineal organ reflects piecemeal rather than dramatic change.

As more Canowindridae or similar fossils are found in Antarctica and Australia, researchers could build a timeline of neuroanatomical changes. Improved scanning techniques and comparative studies with living relatives like lungfish or coelacanths might reveal how the tetrapod brain evolved step by step.
